topic.title: HCF and LCM from numbers written as products of prime factors
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One item most series, usually 2-4 marks in the second half of M3: either 'write N as a product of its prime factors' followed by an HCF or LCM part (Summer 2024 Q20), or an LCM word problem whose last line converts the common multiple into packs, pieces or minutes (Summer 2025 Q23). M4 re-uses it as a short opener (Summer 2023 Q9, Summer 2025 Q9, November 2024 Q2).
mustMemorise: HCF = the primes both numbers share, each at its LOWER power
LCM = every prime in either number, each at its HIGHER power
HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers — use it as a check
Cutting or sharing into equal parts is an HCF; events meeting again or matching pack sizes is an LCM
notOnThisSpec: Finding the HCF or LCM of algebraic terms such as 12x³y and 18xy² (not part of M3-NA-01)
The HCF or LCM of three or more numbers is not the pattern CCEA has set in M3; two numbers is the standard
Euclid's algorithm and formal proofs about divisibility (A level)

note.title: HCF and LCM from prime factor form
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: HCF: shared primes at their lower powers
LCM: all primes at their higher powers

notOnThisSpec: Finding the HCF or LCM of algebraic terms such as 12x³y and 18xy² (not part of M3-NA-01)
The HCF or LCM of three or more numbers is not the pattern CCEA has set in M3; two numbers is the standard
Euclid's algorithm and formal proofs about divisibility (A level)

mustBeAbleTo: Write a number such as 550 or 360 as a product of its prime factors, in index form
Read the HCF of two numbers straight from their prime factorisations by taking the lower power of each shared prime
Read the LCM by taking the higher power of every prime that appears in either number
Decide from the wording whether a word problem wants the HCF (cutting or sharing into equal parts) or the LCM (events coinciding, matching pack sizes)
Convert the common multiple into the quantity the question actually asks for: packs, pieces, minutes and seconds
Check an answer with HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers
sheet.howExamined: M3 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks) and again in M7 Paper 1 with no calculator. Usually one item of 2-4 marks in the second half of the paper: a two-part 'write as a product of prime factors' then 'find the HCF' (Summer 2024 Q20, 2 + 2), or a single LCM word problem of 3 marks whose final mark is for turning the common multiple into packs or minutes (Summer 2025 Q23). Schemes give MA1 for the factorisations or the list of multiples, MA1 for the HCF or LCM itself, and a final A1 for the quantity asked for.
traps: Giving the LCM when the HCF is asked, or the reverse — reported in Summer 2024 M3 Q20(b), where the HCF came back as 630, and again in M4 Q5(b)
Stopping at the common multiple instead of dividing it into packs, pieces or minutes (Summer 2025 M3 Q23; M4 Q9 left as 132)
Using the higher power of a shared prime for the HCF, so the answer does not divide either number (November 2024 M4 Q2)
Multiplying the two numbers and calling it the LCM: that counts every shared prime twice
Stopping a factor tree at 36 × 10 or 2 × 275 instead of splitting down to primes (Summer 2023 M4 Q9)

workedExamples.stem:
$84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$ and $90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5$.

Find the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple of 84 and 90.

figure.alt: Two overlapping circles. The left-only region holds the primes 2 and 7, the overlap holds 2 and 3, the right-only region holds 3 and 5. Labels read 84 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 and 90 = 2 x 3 x 3 x 5.

steps.working: Write each number as a list of primes: $84 = 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 7$, $90 = 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5$
steps.decision: Index form is compact, but a plain list makes the matching visible. Every prime in the list has to be placed somewhere in the diagram exactly once.

steps.working: Shared primes (one 2 and one 3) go in the overlap. What is left over goes outside: 2 and 7 on the 84 side, 3 and 5 on the 90 side.
steps.decision: 84 has two 2s and 90 has one, so only one 2 can be shared; the spare 2 belongs to 84 alone. The same logic puts the spare 3 on the 90 side.

options: Because the overlap can only hold as many copies of a prime as the number with fewer of them has
Because the overlap always holds one copy of every prime that appears
Because 84 is the larger power so it keeps both of its 2s
whyMenu.explain: A common factor has to divide both numbers, so it can use a prime only as many times as the smaller supply allows.

steps.decision: The HCF is the overlap multiplied out. Nothing outside the overlap can be in it, because those primes are missing from one of the two numbers.
The LCM is everything in the diagram: the overlap once, plus each outside region. Written in index form that is $2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7$, the highest power of each prime.

options: The overlap is used once, not twice, because the shared primes are the same primes
The overlap is used twice, once for each circle
The overlap is left out of the LCM
whyMenu.explain: $84 \times 90 = 7560$ counts the shared factor 6 twice; dividing by that 6 gives 1260.

twin.stem: $100 = 2^2 \times 5^2$ and $120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5$. Find the lowest common multiple of 100 and 120.

workedExamples.stem:
Stickers are sold in strips of 15. Reward cards are sold in packs of 25.

Mr Hanna needs the same number of stickers as reward cards, with none left over, and he wants to buy as few as possible.

How many strips of stickers does he buy?

steps.decision: Same number of each, none left over, as few as possible: that is the lowest common multiple. Prime factors first, so the LCM is read off rather than guessed.
Highest power of each prime: one 3 and two 5s. So 75 stickers and 75 cards is the smallest matching total.
The question asks for strips, not stickers. This is the division the examiners keep reporting as the missing last line.

options: 75 is the number of stickers; dividing by 15 turns it into strips
75 is already the number of strips
The number of strips is 75 x 15
whyMenu.explain: The LCM answers 'how many stickers'; one more division answers the question that was asked.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: 5 strips (75 stickers and 3 packs of cards)

twin.stem: Pens come in boxes of 12 and pen lids come in bags of 20. Ciara wants equal numbers of pens and lids with none left over, buying as few as possible. How many boxes of pens does she buy?

items.stem: $\text{Given } 45 = 3^2 \times 5 \text{ and } 60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\text{, what is the HCF of 45 and 60?}$
items.skill: Read the HCF from two prime factorisations

options.feedback: Both numbers contain a 3 and a 5, and nothing else in common, so the HCF is 3 x 5 = 15.
That is the LCM. The HCF is the product of only the primes both numbers share, so it is never larger than either number.
45 uses two 3s but 60 has only one, so the second 3 cannot be in a common factor. Take the lower power of each shared prime.

items.stem: $\text{Given } 45 = 3^2 \times 5 \text{ and } 60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\text{, what is the LCM of 45 and 60?}$
items.skill: Read the LCM from two prime factorisations

options.feedback: Highest power of each prime: 2² x 3² x 5 = 180. It is a multiple of both, and the smallest one.
That is 45 x 60. Multiplying the numbers always gives a common multiple, but the shared factor 15 has been counted twice, so it is 15 times too big.
That is the HCF. A common multiple has to be at least as large as each number.

items.stem: $\text{Two numbers are } 2^3 \times 5^2 \times 7 \text{ and } 2^5 \times 5 \times 11\text{. Which power of 2 goes in the HCF?}$
items.skill: Choose the lower power of a shared prime for the HCF

options.feedback: The first number contains only three 2s, so a common factor cannot use more than three. Lowest power for the HCF.
2⁵ = 32 does not divide the first number, so it cannot be a common factor. Highest power is the LCM rule, not the HCF rule.
The indices were added, which is the rule for multiplying the two numbers together. For the HCF, compare the powers and keep the lower.

items.stem: Buns come in packs of 8 and burgers in packs of 6. Sean wants equal numbers with none left over, buying as few as possible. How many **packs of buns** does he buy?
items.skill: Answer the question asked after finding the LCM

options.feedback: LCM(8, 6) = 24, so 24 of each; packs of buns = 24 ÷ 8 = 3. The division at the end is the mark most often lost.
24 is the number of buns, not the number of packs. One more division turns the common multiple into the answer the question asked for.
4 is the number of packs of burgers (24 ÷ 6). Check which item the question names before writing the answer.

items.stem: Two ribbons, 126 cm and 198 cm, are cut into equal whole-centimetre pieces with none wasted. What is the **longest** each piece can be?
items.skill: Recognise an HCF problem from its wording

options.feedback: 126 = 2 x 3² x 7 and 198 = 2 x 3² x 11, so the HCF is 2 x 9 = 18. 'Longest equal piece, nothing wasted' is always the HCF.
That is the LCM, which is longer than either ribbon, so no piece could be that size. 'Cut into equal pieces' means a common factor.
9 divides both, but so does 18, and the question asks for the longest. The shared 2 has been left out.

parts.stem:
$45 = 3^2 \times 5$ and $60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5$

Write down the highest common factor of 45 and 60.
hints: Which primes appear in both lists?
One 3 and one 5 are in both; 45 has no 2s at all.
parts.workedSolution: Both numbers contain a 3 and a 5. 45 has a second 3 that 60 does not, and 60 has 2s that 45 does not. $\text{HCF} = 3 \times 5 = 15$.

commonErrors.feedback: 180 is the lowest common multiple. The highest common factor divides into both numbers, so it can never be bigger than 45.

questions.solutionProgram: shared primes of 3^2*5 and 2^2*3*5 = 3 and 5; HCF = 3*5 = 15; gcd(45,60) = 15

parts.stem:
$45 = 3^2 \times 5$ and $60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5$

Find the lowest common multiple of 45 and 60.

scheme.for: highest power of each prime seen: 2² × 3² × 5 (or an equivalent list 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5)

hints: Take every prime that appears in either list.
For a prime in both lists, keep the higher power: 3² beats 3.

commonErrors.feedback: $45 \times 60 = 2700$ is a common multiple, but not the lowest: the shared factor 15 has been counted twice. Dividing by 15 gives 180.

context.setting: Pure number, two factorisations given, two parts

parts.stem:
$84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$ and $126 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7$

Find the highest common factor of 84 and 126.

scheme.for: lowest power of each shared prime identified: 2 × 3 × 7

hints: Three primes appear in both: 2, 3 and 7.
84 has one 3 and 126 has one 2, so only one of each can be shared.
parts.workedSolution: Shared primes at their lower powers: $2 \times 3 \times 7 = 42$.

commonErrors.feedback: That uses the higher power of 2 and of 3, which is the LCM rule. A common factor may only use a prime as often as the number with fewer copies of it.

parts.stem: Find the lowest common multiple of 84 and 126.

scheme.for: highest power of each prime seen: 2² × 3² × 7

hints: Every prime in either list, at its higher power.
Or use HCF × LCM = 84 × 126.

commonErrors.feedback: 42 is the answer to part (a). The multiple has to be a number both 84 and 126 divide into, so it is larger than both.

context.setting: Pure number, large numbers given only in index form

parts.stem:
$A = 2^2 \times 5^3 \times 11$ and $B = 2^4 \times 5 \times 11^2$

Write down the highest common factor of $A$ and $B$ in index form.

scheme.for: lower power of at least two of the three primes chosen

hints: Compare the powers prime by prime and keep the lower one each time.
For 2: min(2, 4). For 5: min(3, 1). For 11: min(1, 2).
parts.workedSolution: Lower power of each shared prime: $2^2$, $5^1$, $11^1$, so the HCF is $2^2 \times 5 \times 11 = 220$.

commonErrors.feedback: The higher power was taken each time, which builds the LCM. Keeping the lower power gives 2² × 5 × 11.

parts.stem: Write down the lowest common multiple of $A$ and $B$ in index form.

scheme.for: higher power of at least two of the three primes chosen

hints: Same three primes, higher power each time.
Leaving it in index form is safer than multiplying out.

commonErrors.feedback: $A \times B$ adds the indices, so every shared factor is counted twice. The LCM takes the higher power, not the sum.

emphasis: as a product of its prime factors

context.setting: Pure number, one number must be factorised first

parts.stem: Express 360 as a product of its prime factors. Give your answer in index form.

scheme.for: a correct factor tree or repeated division reaching 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5

hints: Divide by 2 as long as you can, then by 3, then by 5.

commonErrors.feedback: 36 and 10 are factors but not prime factors. Keep splitting until every number left is prime.

parts.stem:
$84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$

Find the highest common factor of 360 and 84.

scheme.for: shared primes at their lower powers: 2² × 3

hints: Use your answer to part (a) and compare it with 2² × 3 × 7.
7 is only in 84, and 5 is only in 360, so neither can be in the HCF.
parts.workedSolution: $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$ and $84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$. Shared: $2^2$ and $3$, so the HCF is 12.

commonErrors.feedback: 84 contains a 7, and 360 does not, so 84 cannot divide 360. Cross out any prime that is missing from one of the lists.

parts.stem:
$96 = 2^5 \times 3$ and $108 = 2^2 \times 3^3$

Work out the highest common factor of 96 and 108.
hints: Lower power of 2, lower power of 3.

commonErrors.feedback: The higher powers were used, giving the LCM. The HCF has to divide 96, and 864 does not.

parts.stem: Work out the lowest common multiple of 96 and 108.
hints: Higher power of 2, higher power of 3.
$32 \times 27$: double 27 five times.

commonErrors.feedback: $96 \times 108$ is a common multiple but counts the shared 12 twice. Dividing by 12 gives 864.

context.setting: Two safety lights on a harbour wall

parts.stem:
Two safety lights on a harbour wall are switched on at the same moment.

The first light flashes every 18 seconds. The second flashes every 24 seconds.

Work out how long it is before both lights flash at the same moment once more. Give your answer in minutes and seconds.

scheme.for: 18 = 2 × 3² and 24 = 2³ × 3, or a list of multiples of both

hints: Together again means a time that is a multiple of both 18 and 24.
72 seconds still has to be written in minutes and seconds.
parts.workedSolution: $18 = 2 \times 3^2$ and $24 = 2^3 \times 3$, so the LCM is $2^3 \times 3^2 = 72$ seconds. $72 = 60 + 12$, so they flash together after 1 minute 12 seconds.

commonErrors.feedback: 72 seconds is right, and it earns two of the three marks. The last mark is for writing it as 1 minute 12 seconds, because the question asks for minutes and seconds.
6 is the highest common factor. The lights coincide at a common multiple, so the number you want is larger than both 18 and 24.

context.setting: Two lengths of ribbon cut for a craft class

parts.stem:
Two lengths of ribbon measure 126 cm and 198 cm.

They are cut into equal pieces, each a whole number of centimetres, with no ribbon wasted.

Calculate the longest possible length of each piece.

scheme.for: 126 = 2 × 3² × 7 and 198 = 2 × 3² × 11 (or a correct factor list for both)

hints: Equal pieces, nothing wasted: the length has to divide both numbers.
Longest possible means the highest such number.
parts.workedSolution: $126 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7$ and $198 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 11$. Shared: $2 \times 3^2 = 18$. Each piece is 18 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: 1386 is the lowest common multiple, and it is longer than either ribbon. Cutting into equal pieces is always a common factor.

parts.stem: Calculate the total number of pieces obtained.
hints: Divide each ribbon by the length you found.
Add the two counts.

commonErrors.feedback: 7 is the number of pieces from the first ribbon only. The question asks for the total, so the 11 pieces from the second ribbon are added.

context.setting: Reasoning about two numbers given only in index form

parts.stem:
$P = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5$ and $Q = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5^2$

Find the highest common factor of $P$ and $Q$.
hints: Lower power of each of the three primes.
min(3, 1) = 1 for the 2s.

commonErrors.feedback: The higher power of each prime gives the LCM. For the HCF, take the lower power each time.

parts.stem:
Rory says that the lowest common multiple of $P$ and $Q$ is $P \times Q$.

Explain why he is not correct, and write down the correct lowest common multiple.

accepted: P × Q counts the shared factors twice; LCM = 1800
LCM = 1800 because P × Q = 54 000 is 30 times too big

scheme.for: a reason referring to the shared factor being counted twice, or to P × Q ÷ HCF

hints: $P \times Q$ is certainly a common multiple. Is it the lowest?
Each of 2, 3 and 5 is in both numbers, so multiplying uses each of them once too often.
$P \times Q \div \text{HCF} = 54\,000 \div 30$.
parts.workedSolution: $P \times Q = 120 \times 450 = 54\,000$, which is a common multiple but not the lowest: every prime shared by $P$ and $Q$ has been counted twice. Taking the higher power of each prime gives $\text{LCM} = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 = 1800$, and indeed $54\,000 \div 30 = 1800$.

commonErrors.feedback: Agreeing with Rory earns nothing. $P \times Q$ is always a common multiple; the lowest one divides it by the HCF, giving 1800.

context.setting: Ordering badges and lanyards for a school open evening

parts.stem:
Name badges are sold in packs of 24. Lanyards are sold in packs of 18.

For an open evening the office needs the same number of badges as lanyards, with none left over. They buy as few packs as possible.

Work out how many **packs of name badges** they buy.

scheme.for: 24 = 2³ × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3², or lists of multiples of 24 and 18

scheme.examinerNote: 72 alone, or 4 (packs of lanyards), scores a maximum of MA1 MA2.

hints: Same number of each with none left over means a common multiple of 24 and 18.
As few as possible means the lowest common multiple.
72 is the number of badges. How many packs of 24 is that?
parts.workedSolution: $24 = 2^3 \times 3$ and $18 = 2 \times 3^2$, so $\text{LCM} = 2^3 \times 3^2 = 72$. That is 72 badges and 72 lanyards. Packs of badges $= 72 \div 24 = 3$ (and 4 packs of lanyards).

commonErrors.feedback: 72 is the number of badges, and it earns the first two marks. The answer line wants packs, so divide by 24 once more. This exact stopping point was reported in Summer 2025 M3 Q23.
4 is the number of packs of lanyards. The bold words in the stem name the item the marker wants counted.
6 is the highest common factor of 24 and 18. Buying the same number of each with none left over needs a common multiple, not a common factor.

emphasis: as a product of its prime factors

context.setting: Pure number, three-part structure in the style of a late M3 question

parts.stem: Write 550 as a product of its prime factors.

scheme.for: correct method seen: a factor tree or repeated division reaching 2, 5, 5, 11

hints: 550 is even, so start by halving it.
275 ends in 5, so divide by 5.
55 = 5 × 11 and 11 is prime.

commonErrors.feedback: Those are factors, but 275, 55 and 10 are not prime. Keep splitting until nothing can be split again.

parts.stem:
$396 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 11$

Find the highest common factor of 550 and 396.

scheme.for: shared primes 2 and 11 identified at their lower powers

hints: Compare your answer to part (a) with 2² × 3² × 11.
550 has only one 2; 396 has no 5s.
parts.workedSolution: $550 = 2 \times 5^2 \times 11$ and $396 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 11$. Shared: one 2 and one 11, so the HCF is $2 \times 11 = 22$.

commonErrors.feedback: 9900 is the lowest common multiple. The examiners report this swap every series: the highest common factor divides both numbers, so it is at most 396.

parts.stem: Find the lowest common multiple of 550 and 396.
hints: Take the higher power of every prime that appears in either number.
Or use: HCF × LCM = 550 × 396.
parts.workedSolution: Higher power of each prime: $2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 \times 11 = 4 \times 9 \times 25 \times 11 = 9900$. Check: $550 \times 396 \div 22 = 217\,800 \div 22 = 9900$.

commonErrors.feedback: $550 \times 396$ counts the shared factor 22 twice. Dividing by the HCF gives 9900.

findTheMistake.stem: Tea lights are sold in boxes of 20 and holders in boxes of 35. Nuala wants equal numbers of each, with none left over, buying as few as possible. She was asked how many **boxes of tea lights** she buys. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: 140 is the number of tea lights, not the number of boxes. The question names boxes of tea lights, so the common multiple still has to be divided by 20.
findTheMistake.feedback: The prime factors and the lowest common multiple are both correct, so two of the three marks stand. The last mark is one division away. Summer 2025 M3 Q23 was reported as exactly this: candidates found the common multiple and wrote it on the answer line instead of the quantity asked for. Read the answer line first, then check what unit it wants.

prompts.prompt: From two prime factorisations, how do you build the HCF and how do you build the LCM?
prompts.answer: HCF: keep only the primes that appear in both, each at its lower power, and multiply. LCM: keep every prime that appears in either, each at its higher power, and multiply.

prompts.prompt: What does 'highest common factor' mean in words?
prompts.answer: The largest number that divides exactly into both numbers. It is never larger than the smaller of the two.

prompts.prompt: What does 'lowest common multiple' mean in words?
prompts.answer: The smallest number that both numbers divide into exactly. It is never smaller than the larger of the two.

prompts.prompt: A question says 'as few as possible, none left over'. HCF or LCM?
prompts.answer: LCM. Sharing out or cutting into equal pieces is the HCF; repeating events meeting again, or buying matching quantities, is the LCM.
$a \times b$. It is a quick check: once you have the HCF, the LCM is $a \times b$ divided by it.

prompts.prompt: You found the lowest common multiple of the two pack sizes. What is the very next thing to do?
prompts.answer: Read the answer line again. If it asks for packs, boxes, strips or minutes, divide or convert; the common multiple on its own is usually not the answer.

prompts.prompt: $A = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 7$ and $B = 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 5$. Write the HCF and the LCM in index form.
